answer.label: Not documented from Picasso — an apocryphal attribution
answer.authorDates: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter, sculptor & co-founder of Cubism
answer.sourceLine: No speech, interview, letter, or book by Picasso has ever been shown to contain this line. Its earliest known link to him is a source-less epigraph in Time magazine in October 1976 — more than three years after his death — and Wikiquote lists it as disputed. The idea that every child is an artist was a commonplace of art writing for decades before Picasso’s name was attached to it.

source.excerpt: Every child is an artist. The problem is how to remain an artist once we grow up.
trail: The earliest known tie to Picasso is a bare epigraph in Time magazine, October 1976, printed with no source or context — over three years after Picasso died in April 1973.
Wikiquote places the line in its “Disputed” section, citing only that same 1976 Time appearance.
The thought long predates Picasso’s name: art critic Carleton Noyes wrote “The child is the first artist” in 1907, and near-identical phrasings recur from 1915 onward, per Quote Investigator.
Quote Investigator searched Picasso’s 1973 obituaries and found no such statement, and does not know where the Time writer got it.
source.excerptNote: The wording circulates in several forms — “once he grows up,” “once we grow up,” “once he or she grows up” — a fingerprint of a saying passed by repetition rather than from a fixed printed source.

source.rightsNote: Because no documented Picasso source for this exact line exists — it first appears posthumously in 1976 with no attribution — there is no identifiable work or first-publication date to which copyright could attach, so rights status cannot be asserted. This is an honest “uncertain,” not a claim of public domain.

author.name: Pablo Picasso
author.heading: About Pablo Picasso
author.metaLine: 1881–1973 · Spanish painter, sculptor & co-founder of Cubism
author.bio: Pablo Picasso (1881–1973) was a Spanish artist whose Cubist innovations and prolific output made him one of the most influential figures in twentieth-century art. He genuinely admired the directness of children’s drawing — famously remarking that it took him years to learn to paint like a child — which is part of why this feel-good line attaches so easily to his name. But admiration for children’s art is not the same as authorship of this particular sentence, and no source in his own words has ever been found.

copyAttribution: Widely attributed to Pablo Picasso, but disputed — no primary source exists; the line first appears in Time magazine in 1976, three years after his death.

misattribution.heading: Why this one is disputed
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s most-shared “Picasso” quotes, yet its trail runs cold at a posthumous magazine epigraph — and the underlying idea belonged to no single author.

items.who: No documented source in Picasso’s own words
items.why: Quote Investigator found the earliest Picasso attribution in Time magazine, October 1976 — printed with no source, three-plus years after Picasso’s 1973 death — and located nothing in his obituaries or writings.

items.who: Carleton Noyes, Percy Mackaye, and others
items.why: The claim that every child is an artist was a stock theme long before Picasso’s name attached to it: critic Carleton Noyes wrote “The child is the first artist” in 1907, and ‘Every child is an artist’ recurs from 1915 onward.

misattribution.truthLine: Both specialist trackers converge: Wikiquote calls it disputed and Quote Investigator finds no primary source — so treat it as apocryphal, not verified Picasso.

context.heading: A quote that sounds right
lead: Picasso really did revere the unschooled boldness of children’s art, which is exactly why this sentence sticks to him so effortlessly — it flatters both the artist and the reader. That plausibility is the engine of misattribution: a line that feels like something Picasso would say needs no citation to travel.

But feeling right is not evidence. The paper trail begins in 1976, after Picasso could no longer confirm or deny it, and the thought itself had been in circulation for nearly seventy years under other names.
context.pull: It sounds like Picasso — which is precisely why no one checked.
